mappings.note: Picks the most accurate written representation of a neutralisation. Equation-writing for neutralisation, C 1.3-LO-3 exactly.
Which acid is not a mineral acid. Mineral-versus-organic classification has no outcome here; competency cited, as with 84970, which this duplicates.
Which listed substance is not a base. Deciding what counts as a base, LO-3.
Which statement is true for acids (sour, turn blue litmus red). Indicator-based characterisation, LO-3.
Picks the correct chlor-alkali equation. Equation-writing, but electrolysis rather than a neutralisation or acid-on-metal, so the competency rather than C 1.3-LO-3.
Identify the basic salt. The pH of a salt solution, LO-4.
Identify the basic salt. Same demand as 149827, which it duplicates; the frame offers nothing finer than LO-4 for either.
Blue litmus in acid turns red. Indicator behaviour, LO-3.
Names three acid-base indicators. LO-3.
Colour changes of litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein in acid and base. LO-3's indicator clause in full.
True/false on phenolphthalein being pink in acid. Indicator colours, LO-3.
Red litmus turns blue in base. Indicator behaviour, LO-3.
Matches four indicators to their colour in base. LO-3.
pH of a neutral solution is 7. The pH scale, LO-4.
Assertion-reason tying pH 3 to acidity via the below-7 rule. The pH scale, LO-4.
The pH scale runs to 14. LO-4.
Full account of what pH measures, its range and what values mean. The fullest LO-4 item in the chapter.
pH 2 versus pH 6 as a factor of ten thousand in H+. The logarithmic pH scale, LO-4.
Gas from dilute sulphuric acid on zinc. The acid-metal reaction of LO-3.
Observations for dilute HCl on zinc granules and the pop test. LO-3; the equation appears in the answer but is not what the stem asks for.
Labelled gas-collection apparatus for acid on metal, plus the test. The chemistry is LO-3; setting up and using the apparatus is C 8.2 (its LO-1 is about pH testing, which this is not).
Chemical name of baking soda. LO-5's substance.
True/false on baking soda raising cakes by releasing CO2. A use and property of baking soda, LO-5.
Preparation, properties and uses of baking soda with equations. LO-5 word for word.
A white powder giving a lime-water-milky gas with acid must be a carbonate. The acid-carbonate reaction of LO-3.
What makes an acid strong -- complete ionisation. Strength as H+ concentration, LO-4.
Whether a dilute strong acid can have the higher pH. Separates strength from concentration on the pH scale, LO-4.
Assertion-reason on concentrated meaning strong -- false. Strength versus concentration, LO-4.
Full distinction between strength and concentration and why confusing them is unsafe. LO-4.
Ten water molecules in washing soda. The formula of an LO-5 substance.
Water of crystallisation explained through blue vitriol. Copper sulphate is not one of LO-5's four substances, so the competency is cited, consistently with the other blue-vitriol items.
Assertion-reason on blue vitriol crystals being wet -- false, the water is chemically combined. Same reading as 706920; blue vitriol is outside LO-5.
Mass and percentage of water of crystallisation lost by blue vitriol. Numerical, and again outside LO-5's four substances; competency cited.
Tooth decay begins below pH 5.5. An everyday-pH threshold, LO-4.
Three everyday consequences of pH with the chemistry of each. LO-4's application clause.
An oxide reacting with both acids and bases is amphoteric. Acid-base character of oxides, LO-3.
Why metal oxides count as basic -- they neutralise acids (LO-3) -- with the balanced equation the question demands (C 1.3-LO-3).
Hydrogen at the cathode in the chlor-alkali process. Brine electrolysis is the industrial-chemicals section LO-5 covers, its products feeding bleaching powder and washing soda.
Why the process is called chlor-alkali and what its three products are used for. Preparation and uses of LO-5's industrial chemicals.
Labelled diagram of brine electrolysis with all three products. Same LO-5 ground as 706927; it is a recall diagram, not an investigation, so C 8.2 is not cited.
What an olfactory indicator is, with an example. Indicators, LO-3.
The general word equation for neutralisation. Writing the neutralisation equation, C 1.3-LO-3.
True/false on neutralisation always giving salt and water. The reaction described, LO-3; nothing is written as an equation.
Confirm acidic soil, advise a remedy, explain the chemistry. Sampling and pH-testing systematically is C 8.2-LO-1; reading the pH is LO-4; liming as an acid-base reaction is LO-3.
Experiment showing neutralisation is exothermic and destroys both sets of properties. The chemistry is LO-3; designing and running the calorimetric test is C 8.2.
Why plaster of Paris needs a dry container. A property of plaster of Paris, LO-5. (Duplicates 84938 -- see defect list.)
Gypsum heated to about 100 degrees gives plaster of Paris. Preparation, LO-5.
Why concentrated acid goes into water and never the reverse. The exothermic dilution of an acid has no outcome in this frame; competency cited, as with 84916.
pH 4 is acidic and ten times more so than pH 5. The logarithmic pH scale, LO-4.
Dry HCl gas leaves litmus alone because no ions form without water. LO-4's H+ basis.
Formula and a use of bleaching powder. LO-5 names it.
Why sodium carbonate solution is basic despite being a salt. The pH of a salt solution, LO-4.
True/false on all salt solutions being neutral. The pH of salt solutions, LO-4.
Why non-metal oxides count as acidic -- they neutralise bases (LO-3) -- with the equation the question requires (C 1.3-LO-3).
Names the parent acid and base of three salts (LO-3, neutralisation read backwards) and follows through to whether each solution is neutral or not (LO-4).
Matches baking soda, washing soda, bleaching powder and plaster of Paris to their formulae. LO-5's four substances exactly.
Assertion-reason on all bases being alkalis -- false, only the soluble ones are. Defining bases, LO-3.
Washing soda is Na2CO3.10H2O. The formula of an LO-5 substance.
